story: Uta-napishtim, a mortal king of the city of Shuruppak, was tasked by the god Enki to abandon his possessions and build a giant ship called Preserver of Life to survive a coming flood that would destroy all life. The ship was made of solid timber so sunlight would not shine in, equal in length and width, its design drawn on the ground by Enki. The frame was built in five days, measuring 200 feet in length, width, and height, with a floor-space of one acre. It had seven floors, each divided into nine sections, and was finished on the seventh day. Once everyone had boarded, the entrance was sealed. Uta-napishtim brought his wife, family, relatives, craftsmen of his village, baby animals, and grains aboard. The flood wiped out all who were not on the ship. After twelve days on the water, Uta-napishtim opened the hatch and saw the slopes of Mount Nisir, where he rested the ship for seven days. He sent out a dove, which found nothing and returned; then a swallow, which also returned; finally a raven, which saw the waters had receded and did not return. Uta-napishtim freed the animals and made a sacrifice to the gods. Because he had preserved mankind's seed and remained loyal, the gods granted Uta-napishtim and his wife immortality and a place among the heavenly gods. Later, the hero Gilgamesh, mourning his friend Enkidu, sought out Uta-napishtim to learn the secret of eternal life. Uta-napishtim told him to abandon his quest, then set him a trial to stay awake, which Gilgamesh failed. Uta-napishtim then revealed a plant that could restore youth. Gilgamesh retrieved it from the sea bottom, but a serpent stole it, and he returned home without immortality or renewed youth.
